usage: Plain first-person pronoun used down or sideways: to close friends, younger people, or family. Never up to elders.
나 + 가 fuses to 내가, never '나가.' This shape change is irregular and must be memorized.
나 + 는 marks the topic ('as for me'); shortened to 난 in fast speech and texting.
나 + 도 ('also'); the everyday way to say 'me too' among friends, e.g. 나도 갈래.
examples: Pure 반말: bare 나 with no particle, the most casual register among close friends.
Can you give this to me?
나 here is the recipient ('to me'); the bare pronoun stands in for 나한테 in relaxed speech.
Real-situation promise: 나 must become 내 before 가, giving the subject 내가.
nuance: 나 is the plain, intimate word for 'I/me' — the counterpart of the humble 저. Choosing between them is not about meaning but about RELATIONSHIP and DIRECTION: 나 points downward or sideways (to friends, juniors, family), while 저 lowers you toward someone you respect; saying 나 to a boss or stranger sounds blunt or rude. 나 carries a warm, unguarded feel, so it dominates 반말 and shows up constantly in 나도 (me too), 나는 (as for me), 내 거 (mine). The classic English-speaker pitfall is the subject form: English keeps 'I' fixed, but Korean fuses 나 + 가 into 내가 — '나가' actually reads as the verb 'go out,' so it is not just wrong but confusing. Also resist supplying a pronoun for every English 'I'; Koreans drop it whenever context is clear.

usage: Plain second-person pronoun, safe only with close friends and people clearly younger than you.
너 + 가 becomes written 네가, but almost everyone says 니가 out loud to avoid clashing with 내가.
너 + 는 ('as for you'); contracts to 넌 in speech, e.g. 넌 어때?
너 + 도; the casual 'you too,' as in 너도 올래? (Want to come too?).
examples: Bare 너 in 반말; texting a close friend, no politeness ending at all.
너 + 도 ('you too') checking a shared taste between friends.
Real exchange: subject form 네가 (said 니가) telling a friend to go ahead.
nuance: 너 is the plain 'you,' the partner of 나, and is genuinely usable only downward or among intimates — close friends, a younger sibling, a child. The crucial difference from English is that Korean has no neutral, all-purpose 'you': to elders, strangers, coworkers, or anyone you respect, 너 sounds disrespectful or even hostile, so Koreans switch to the person's name + 씨/님, a role word (선생님, 사장님), or simply drop 'you' entirely. Note the famous subject form: 너 + 가 is written 네가 but pronounced 니가 in real life, because 네가 and 내가 (I) collapse to the same sound otherwise. The big pitfall is mapping English 'you' straight onto 너 — pointing 너 at a waiter or a senior is a real social error; default to a name or title and let context carry the rest.

Writing '너가' for the subject; the standard written form is 네가 (commonly said 니가).
Translating every English 'you' as 너 — in polite Korean the 'you' word is usually omitted or replaced by a name.

usage: Humble first-person pronoun; the safe default with elders, strangers, customers, and in formal settings.
저 + 가 fuses to 제가, never '저가.' Use it to volunteer or take responsibility politely.
저 + 는; the standard opener for introducing yourself: 저는 ...이에요/입니다.
humble 'we'; 저희 회사, 저희 집 politely lowers your own group toward the listener.
examples: Simple self-introduction; 저 + 는 paired with the polite 요-form.
Everyday offer at work: subject 제가 plus the humble 도와드리다 to lift the listener.
Nice to meet you, I'm Kim Minsu.
Real first meeting in 격식체 (formal -ㅂ니다); 저 is obligatory here.
nuance: 저 is the humble 'I/me,' the polite counterpart of 나. It does not mean something different from 나 — it encodes DEFERENCE, lowering yourself to raise the listener, so it is the correct choice with elders, strangers, customers, and any formal moment, and it sits naturally with 요-form and -ㅂ니다 speech. Like 나 it has an irregular subject form: 저 + 가 fuses to 제가, not '저가.' Two traps for English speakers: first, the homograph — this 저 (I) is spelled identically to the demonstrative 저 'that (over there),' but sentence position keeps them apart; second, the humble plural 저희 ('we/our'), which has no English equivalent and which learners forget, defaulting to plain 우리 even when politely referring to their own company or family. When in doubt about register, 저 is the safer pronoun.

usage: Sino-Korean 當身; a 'high' you that, said to a stranger's face, often reads as cold or confrontational.
당신 + 이 (consonant ending takes 이, not 가); appears in lyrics, vows, and between spouses.
당신 + 은; common in ads and self-help writing that address 'you, the reader.'
당신 + 을; literary and romantic, as in 당신을 사랑해요.
examples: Affectionate spousal use; in songs and marriage 당신 is warm, not cold.
Ad / writing voice addressing an unseen reader as 당신.
Who are you to talk to me like that?
Real argument: the same 당신 turns sharp and confrontational toward a stranger.
nuance: 당신 is a formal 'you' from the Sino-Korean 當身 (當 'this/that', 身 'body/self'), and it is one of the most misleading words for learners. Unlike a flat English 'you,' 당신 has split lives: warm and intimate between spouses ('dear/honey'), poetic in lyrics and prayer, and reader-facing in ads or essays — yet aimed at a stranger's face in conversation it sounds cold, distancing, or like the opening of a fight (it is a staple of street arguments). So although dictionaries gloss it as 'you,' it is NOT the everyday polite 'you'; the honest truth is Korean has no neutral spoken 'you' at all. The pitfall is reaching for 당신 to a clerk, a senior, or a new acquaintance the way you'd say 'you' in English — instead use the person's name + 씨/님, a title (선생님, 사장님, 손님), or drop the word entirely. Reserve 당신 for writing, lyrics, or your own spouse.

Writing '당신가' for the subject — 당신 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이: 당신이.

usage: The standard, respectful word for one's father, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 지 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 아버지예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 아버지 + 님; used for another person's father or one's father-in-law.
examples: My father is an office worker.
Note 우리 ('our') for 'my' family member — Koreans rarely say 내 아버지.
아버지 as object with 를; pairs with the humble self-pronoun 저.
My father is reading the newspaper.
Full honorific chain: subject 께서 + the honorific verb ending -으세요.
nuance: 아버지 is the respectful, neutral word for 'father,' used in polite conversation, in writing, and whenever you speak about your dad to others. Its near-synonym 아빠 is the warm home word ('dad/daddy'): children and many adults call him 아빠 to his face, while 아버지 sounds more grown-up, dignified, or formal — the gap is exactly the English 'dad' vs 'father.' One step higher is 아버님, reserved for someone else's father or your father-in-law. Because a father is an elder, 아버지 naturally pulls honorific machinery: the subject marker 께서, the dative 께, and -(으)시- verb endings (읽으세요, 주무세요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: the copula is 아버지예요 (vowel-final 지 → 예요, not '아버지이에요'); and possession uses 우리 아버지 ('our father'), since 내 아버지 sounds oddly cold to Korean ears.

usage: The standard, respectful word for one's mother, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 니 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 어머니예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 어머니 + 님; for another person's mother or one's mother-in-law.
examples: Again 우리 ('our') for one's own mother, the natural choice over 내 어머니.
I gave my mother a present.
Honorific dative 께 (not 한테) plus the humble give-verb 드리다.
Real scene: subject 께서 + honorific 하세요 to respect the elder.
nuance: 어머니 is the respectful, neutral word for 'mother,' used in polite speech, in writing, and when talking about your mom to others. Its near-synonym 엄마 is the affectionate home word ('mom/mommy') that people usually call her directly at home, while 어머니 carries more formality and respect — the same distance as English 'mom' vs 'mother.' The higher honorific 어머님 is for someone else's mother or your mother-in-law. Possession is likewise 우리 어머니, since 내 어머니 sounds unnaturally distant.

usage: The bright part of the day, the opposite of 밤 (night).
낮 + 에 marks the time-when; pronounced '나제' from the ㅈ liaison.
낮 + 잠 (sleep) = a daytime sleep; pairs with the verb 자다 (낮잠을 자다).
한 ('full/peak') + 낮 = the hottest, brightest middle of the day.
examples: 낮 + 에 + 는 sets a daytime topic, implying a contrast with night.
I take a nap on weekends.
Everyday habit: the compound 낮잠 with its set verb 자다.
I work in the daytime and study at night.
Real routine contrasting 낮 with its antonym 밤 across one sentence.
nuance: 낮 means the daytime — the bright stretch between morning and evening — and lives as the natural antonym of 밤 (night). It is a pure native Korean noun (not Sino-Korean), and its key feature is pronunciation: the final ㅈ links onto a following vowel, so 낮에 sounds like '나제' and 낮이 like '나지'; before a consonant or pause the ㅈ neutralizes to a 't' sound ('낟'). Its near-synonym 오후 'afternoon' is narrower and Sino-Korean (the clock-time after noon), whereas 낮 is the whole bright span and feels more everyday. The headline English-speaker pitfall is a cluster of look-alikes that differ by one final consonant: 낮 (daytime), 낯 (face, as in 낯설다 'unfamiliar'), and 낫 (a sickle; also 낫다 'to be better / to recover'). They sound nearly identical in isolation, so rely on meaning and the liaison to keep them straight, and pair 낮 with 에 to say 'during the day.'

Treating 낮 and 오후 as identical — 오후 is specifically 'afternoon' (post-noon), while 낮 is the whole bright daytime.

usage: Everyday standalone word for color; feels fuller and warmer than the bare 색.
무슨 + 색깔 asks which color something is: 무슨 색깔이에요?
색깔 + 이 as subject with an adjective; 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular (예뻐요).
set collocation; 진하다 (deep) vs 연하다 (light) describe color intensity.
examples: Simplest color question; 색깔 stands alone naturally as the subject.
This bag has a pretty color.
Real answer: 색깔 as topic, but a specific shade uses 색 inside 파란색.
nuance: 색깔 is the everyday, standalone word for 'color,' built on the Sino-Korean root 색 (色 'color') plus a native suffix that makes it feel fuller and more conversational. Its near-synonym is just 색: the dividing line is grammatical, not meaning — 색깔 stands on its own (색깔이 예뻐요, 무슨 색깔?), while 색 is the building block that fuses to a specific shade name (파란색 blue, 빨간색 red, 노란색 yellow). A more formal, technical synonym is 색상, common in design and shopping ('color option'). The main English-speaker pitfall is over-using 색깔 by sticking it onto shade names — '파란색깔' is wrong; the named colors take 색, giving 파란색. Also, to ask 'what color,' the natural question word is 무슨 색깔, not 어떤 색깔 (which leans toward 'what kind/sort of color').

usage: The standard color noun for green (草綠色); 초록 alone is also common.
color noun + noun, the basic modifier pattern (no extra particle).
I'll take the green one, please
instrumental 으로 ('in the form of') for choosing a color at a store.
a fresh, pale spring green; a distinct shade, not just 'light 초록.'
examples: Naming a favorite color; 초록색 + 을 좋아하다.
Do you have a green umbrella?
Shopping: 초록색 directly modifies 우산 with no particle.
Now that spring has come, the leaves are green.
Real scene: 초록색 + 이에요 describing fresh leaves.
nuance: 초록색 is the standard word for 'green' — the green of leaves and grass. It is Sino-Korean: 草 'grass' + 綠 'green' + 色 'color,' literally 'grass-green color,' which is a handy memory hook. In casual speech people drop 색 and say just 초록 (초록 좋아해), and in fashion you'll also hear the English loan 그린. Its near-synonyms are real shade distinctions, not loose alternatives: 연두색 is a paler, yellowish spring green, and 청록색 is a bluish teal-green — so reserve 초록색 for ordinary mid-green. The standout English-speaker pitfall is the traffic light: a 'green light' is logically 초록불, and that's correct, but by long habit Koreans overwhelmingly call it 파란불 ('blue light'). So a green go-signal is usually 파란불 in everyday speech even though the lamp is green.

usage: The standard color noun for white; 하얀색 is an equally common synonym.
color noun + clothing item, a very common pairing (no particle).
흰색 + 이에요 to state a color (consonant-final 색 → 이에요).
I'll take the white one, please
instrumental 으로 for picking the white option at a store.
examples: Simple statement of color; 흰색 + 이에요.
흰색 directly modifies 운동화; everyday shopping past tense.
흰색하고 검은색 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요?
Between white and black, which do you prefer?
Real choice: 흰색 contrasted with its opposite 검은색 (black).

Its near-synonym 하얀색 (from 하얗다) is just as common and means the same; the nuance is feel — 흰색 is a touch more neutral and matter-of-fact, 하얀색 a touch softer and more vivid. Keep the noun separate from the adjectives that describe whiteness: name the color with 흰색 (흰색 셔츠, 흰색이에요), but describe how white something looks with 하얗다 → 하얘요 (눈이 하얘요 'the snow is white'); 하얗다 is a ㅎ-irregular, hence 하얘요, 하얀. The main English-speaker pitfalls are two near-neighbors: don't blur 흰색 (white) with 회색 (gray, 灰色), which looks and sounds similar, and don't say '하얀색이다' when you mean to describe a thing — use the adjective 하얘요 for that.

structuredNuance.t: 흰색 is the standard color noun for 'white.'

Its near-synonym 하얀색 (from 하얗다) is just as common and means the same; the nuance is feel — 흰색 is a touch more neutral and matter-of-fact, 하얀색 a touch softer and more vivid. Keep the noun separate from the adjectives that describe whiteness: name the color with 흰색 (흰색 셔츠, 흰색이에요), but describe how white something looks with 하얗다 → 하얘요 (눈이 하얘요 'the snow is white'); 하얗다 is a ㅎ-irregular, hence 하얘요, 하얀.
It is built from the native adjective stem 희- (희다 'to be white') plus 색 (色 'color').

Two near-neighbors trip learners up: don't blur 흰색 (white) with 회색 (gray, 灰色), which looks and sounds similar, and don't say '하얀색이다' when you mean to describe a thing — use the adjective 하얘요 for that.

mistakes: Confusing the color noun 흰색 with the adjective 하얗다 — name the color with 흰색, describe whiteness with 하얘요.
Mixing up 흰색 (white) with 회색 (gray, 灰色); they look and sound a bit alike but are different colors.
Mis-conjugating 하얗다 as '하얗어요'; it is a ㅎ-irregular, so the form is 하얘요.

usage: General native word for any alcoholic drink (소주, 맥주, 막걸리...).
술 + 을 with 마시다 (drink), the standard verb — not 먹다.
술 + 집 (house) = a drinking place; the everyday word for a bar.
literally 'do one glass of alcohol'; a warm invitation to drink together.
examples: Simple statement; 술 + 을 + the standard verb 마시다, negated with 안.
Let's grab a drink together today.
Set phrase 술 한잔하다 as a friendly invitation; 잔 is the glass/cup counter.
You have to drive, so please don't drink.
Real caution: 술은 (contrast topic) + polite prohibition -지 마세요.
nuance: 술 is the general native word for any alcoholic drink — the umbrella over 소주, 맥주, 막걸리, 와인, and more. Like other liquids it takes the verb 마시다 'to drink' (술을 마시다), NOT 먹다; in very casual speech you will hear 술을 먹다 too, but 마시다 is the form to learn and use. Beyond the noun, drinking is deeply social in Korea, so 술 anchors set phrases: 술 한잔하다 'to go for a drink' (a friendly invite), 술자리 'a drinking gathering,' 술집 'a bar,' and the morning-after 술이 깨다 'to sober up.' There is also etiquette baked into the word: you pour for others, not yourself, and a junior turns slightly away when drinking before an elder. The big English-speaker pitfall is reflexively pairing 'drink' with 먹다 (which means 'eat'); in careful Korean alcohol is 마시다. Also keep 술 (alcohol) distinct from 물 (water) — they differ by a single vowel.

mistakes: Pairing 술 with 먹다 in careful speech; the standard verb is 마시다 (술을 마셔요).
Confusing 술 (alcohol) with 물 (water) — one vowel apart but very different drinks.
Counting drinks with the wrong counter — a glass of alcohol is 술 한 잔, using the cup/glass counter 잔.

usage: NATIVE number 하나 → 한 before 시. Hours always use native numbers.
NATIVE 둘 → 두 + 시, never '이 시.'
몇 + 시 asks the hour: 몇 시예요? (What time is it?).
the HOUR (시) takes native numbers, the MINUTES (분) take Sino numbers.
examples: Core question; 몇 시 + 예요 asks for the hour.
I get up at seven o'clock.
Native 일곱 + 시 + 에 ('at'); 에 marks clock time.
수업이 세 시 삼십 분에 끝나요.
Mixed systems in one clause: NATIVE 세 시 for the hour, SINO 삼십 분 for the minutes.
nuance: 시 is the counter for the o'clock HOUR (from 時 'time/hour'), and it is one of the great beginner traps because Korean splits its two number systems across the clock: the HOUR uses NATIVE numbers (한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시, 다섯 시...), while the MINUTES counter 분 uses SINO-Korean numbers (일 분, 십 분, 삼십 분). So 3:30 is 세 시 삼십 분 — native for the hour, Sino for the minutes — and mixing them up ('삼 시' or '세십 분') is the classic mistake. Watch the irregular shape changes the native numbers make right before 시: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (스무 시 in 24-hour form). To say 'at' a time, attach 에: 두 시에 'at two o'clock.' Don't confuse the noun 시 'o'clock' with its homophones 시 'poem' (詩) or the city suffix 시 (市, as in 부산시) — the counter use is always preceded by a native number.

mistakes: Using Sino numbers for the hour, e.g. '삼 시' for three o'clock; it must be the native 세 시.
Using native numbers for minutes — 분 takes Sino numbers, so say 삼십 분, never '서른 분' or '세십 분.'
Forgetting the pre-시 shape change: 둘 → 두 시, 셋 → 세 시, not '둘 시' / '셋 시.'
